sum.text:
The dramatic street theatre playing out across the capital – marked by Opposition marches to the Supreme Court, symbolic satyagraha at Rajghat, and viral standoffs with law enforcement – highlights a shift in modern political dissent. In The Revolt of the Public, Martin Gurri analysed how the digital age empowers the Public to rapidly mobilise, not to build alternative institutions, but to aggressively challenge and dismantle existing centres of authority.
The ongoing protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls serve as a textbook manifestation of Gurri’s thesis. By declaring the referee guilty before any judicial or institutional verdict has been rendered, a disparate collective of opposition interests is testing the boundaries of democratic accountability.
A central feature of Gurri’s framework is that the modern Public operates primarily through negation. It is defined by what it opposes rather than what it proposes. In the current controversy, the Indian National Congress and its regional allies have levelled severe allegations of ‘vote theft’ and systematic disenfranchisement. They point to the removal of over 1.3 crore names from draft rolls as definitive proof of manipulation. Conversely, the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the ruling dispensation maintain that this is a routine administrative cleanup aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased, and ineligible entries.
The striking feature of this standoff is not the disagreement itself, but the structural refusal to wait for evidence. In a traditional democratic setup, complex administrative disputes are channelled through institutional arbiters – the Parliament, the judiciary, specialised committees, or independent audits. However, the Opposition’s strategy bypasses these deliberative steps entirely. By demanding the immediate resignation of the CEC, the protest movement operates on a “verdict-first” logic. Guilt is established by public proclamation, and the street becomes the court of first and final resort.
Critics argue that this rush to judgment stems from the political frustration of an Opposition repeatedly bested at the ballot box. When conventional institutional avenues feel blocked, the motivation to delegitimise the institutional framework grows. sum.text: Columbia University, New York: In a much-awaited move, last week, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the sale of a combined 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank held by GoI and LIC to 10955230 Canada Inc, a Canadian subsidiary of Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. The sale would fetch the government ₹26,544 cr and LIC ₹26,335 cr. While some formalities remain before the sale is concluded, the decision can be hailed as a landmark step forward in GoI's larger privatisation programme. Even though IDBI was recategorised as a private sector bank by RBI in 2019 after LIC acquired a 51% controlling stake, its sale is an encouraging sign that PSBs can be sold to foreign buyers, countering the oft-repeated argument that there are not enough potential buyers of Indian banks. Indeed, the sale of IDBI Bank to a Canadian entity comes on the heels of Japan's Konoike Transport Co Ltd's acquisition last year of Ferro Scrap Nigam Ltd, a PSU. Together, these transactions testify to the government's growing comfort with foreign investors as potential buyers of PSUs and PSBs and, conversely, to foreign investors' enhanced appetite for Indian public-sector assets. Integrating even the Indian public sector into the global economy in this manner is essential to modernising the Indian economy, provided national security or strategic concerns are not at stake. After entering RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework in May 2017, IDBI has undergone a remarkable turnaround. Its gross NPAs fell from 21.25%, then to 2.32% in 2025-26, while its capital adequacy ratio rose from 10.7% to 26.65% over the same period. In 2025-26, the bank's total business exceeded ₹6 lakh cr, with net profit reaching a record ₹9,513 cr. This turnaround may have strengthened the hand of privatisation opponents. They will no doubt argue that GoI is selling the family silver to make up for its failure to raise adequate tax revenue, without asking what price the government has paid to keep that silver shining. Over the years, GoI has mobilised substantial taxpayer funds to keep IDBI Bank afloat. Between 2010-11 and 2019-20, infusions into the bank added ₹27,441 cr to the exchequer's bill. In 2017-18 alone, the infusion was ₹12,471 cr. These infusions do not include the ₹26,367 cr that LIC has invested since acquiring control of the bank in January 2019. sum.text:
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, industrial policy has seen a rapid revival, thanks mainly to geopolitical crises spilling over into supply-chain disruptions and China’s surging exports, which are now actively deindustrialising countries as varied as Germany and Thailand. Yet, the rising discussion around and adoption of industrial policy is increasingly decontextualised from the sociopolitical and institutional bargains that underpinned its successful application in East and Southeast Asia. This brief outlines what a classic East Asian developmental state entailed—the bureaucratic, economic, and political arrangements that held it together, and the historical contingencies that made industrial policy work in specific countries.
Going forward, industrial policy can be a highly effective tool for policymakers. However, the concept has to be fundamentally reinterpreted against the current realities of state efficacy and capacity, necessary political capital, global macroeconomic environment, and rapidly evolving geopolitical contours. As the post-World War II order recedes, the political and economic assumptions and certainties that policymakers across the world relied on have considerably weakened.
A 2026 report by Global Trade Alert notes that the ongoing West Asia conflict has resulted in over 500 government actions and policy interventions worldwide. From consumer-friendly subsidies and import quotas to export barriers and austerity measures, governments everywhere are deploying all the policy tools at their disposal to mitigate the effects of the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Amid this frenzy, it is easy to miss some important shifts in the underlying economic policy thinking.
During the summer of 2026, two developments signalled a structural shift in industrial policy and the emergence of a new set of assumptions in the post-postwar era. The first was a new World Bank report that provided a comprehensive guide to deploying industrial policy for development in the 21st century. The second was the European Union’s (EU) plan to relax the regulations for corporate mergers to facilitate EU-based “global champions.” This paper can be accessed here.
This paper is authored by Srijan Shukla, ORF.

points: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navanethem Navi Pillay, marking a bold and historic choice by the Oslo committee.

She has a distinguished legal career, having defended Nelson Mandela during apartheid trials, served as an ICC judge, and as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

This was no ordinary selection. The Nobel Committee in Oslo deciding on the Peace Prize has shown guts in the past, to the world’s applause. It has also shown a lack of this, to the world’s disappointment.
It has often shown a sense of history, especially of history-in-the-making — in its 1964 choice, Martin Luther King Jr., and in its 2014 choice, the 17-year-old Malala Yousafzai. These instances have affirmed the world’s sense of rightness. At the same time, its total lack of such sense and capability has often caused the world to groan: The absence of Mahatma Gandhi from the Nobel Peace Prize list has been written about far too much to bear any repetition.
In any case, it does not behove the India of renunciates to go on and on about it. I will not mention, negatively, any laureate to question the selection. But let facts speak for themselves.
The US, bless that country of pre-Nobel greats such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and Abraham Lincoln, leads all nations with the highest number of Nobel Peace Prize laureates — 27 — out of the total of 113 individuals and 31 organisations. The UK and Switzerland follow, at a respectable distance, with 14 each. Anything not quite right about that accumulation of the medallion?
Of the 27 US nationals who have received the Nobel Peace Prize, four are US Presidents: Theodore Roosevelt (1906), Woodrow Wilson (1919), Jimmy Carter (2002), and Barack Obama (2009). Should that be cause for discomfort? I, for one, rejoiced at Obama’s selection though it felt a tad too early.
So, no; White House incumbency should not disqualify a person from becoming a Nobel laureate. US secretaries of State have done better than US Presidents in the matter of the Peace Prize — Elihu Root (1912), Frank B Kellogg (1929), Cordell Hull (1945), George C Marshall (1953) and, yes, Henry Kissinger (1973). There is more to the Nobel Peace Prize and the US.

Trump, on his Truth Social platform, called it “a wonderful gesture of mutual respect”. It must be said here that the Nobel Committee had nothing to do with this egregious act.

sum.text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may need to raise its benchmark repo rate to at least 6.25 per cent to contain inflation risks, according to SBI Funds Management, an assessment that has gained relevance following the latest rise in retail and wholesale inflation.
In its October 2026 Market Outlook report, the fund house said further monetary tightening could be necessary even after the RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent earlier this month. "From a real rate perspective, policy rates may need to move to at least 6.25% to enable a real rate around 1%," the report stated. The assessment implies another 75 basis points of rate increases from the current level, although the report does not specify a timeline.
The warning comes as India's retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September from 4.83 per cent in August, while wholesale inflation accelerated to 11.39 per cent from 9.92 per cent, according to government data released last week. "Even with the current forward estimate on CPI inflation for FY27 at 5.20%, headline CPI remains almost 120bps above the 4% target. This clearly warrants additional policy actions going forward," the report stated.
The RBI has projected inflation at 6 per cent in the third quarter of FY27 and 5.7 per cent in the fourth quarter, reflecting continued price pressures. SBI Funds Management warned that elevated crude oil prices, potential food inflation and strong domestic demand could push inflation above the RBI's 6 per cent upper tolerance limit for two consecutive quarters. "Accordingly, the near-term path for the policy rates is either a hike or hold with rate cuts being off the table," it said.
The fund house also cautioned that surplus banking-system liquidity could weaken the effectiveness of rate hikes, making liquidity management important for controlling inflation.
The RBI's next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for December 2-4, when it will review fresh inflation data before deciding on further interest rate action.

sum.text:
NEW DELHI: In a significant ruling relating to Prevention of Corruption Act, Supreme Court has said that the shield of prior sanction from higher authorities to prosecute a public servant is not available if they are caught demanding bribes. The court stressed that the statutory protection is meant only to prevent persecution of officials for decisions made in discharge of their duties. The ruling was given by a bench of Justices SVN Bhatti and N V Anjaria while interpreting Section 17A of the Act, which was inserted in the statute in 2018 and prohibited police or investigating agencies from conducting without official approval any inquiry or investigation into alleged offences committed by public servants while discharging their duties.
Dismissing an appeal by a Rajasthan police constable challenging an FIR and chargesheet against him for allegedly demanding a bribe of Rs 1.5 lakh, the bench said the Section 17A shield cannot have an omnibus application to all public servants facing prosecution for criminal offences.“The act of demanding a bribe is a pure criminal act, not connected with official functions and not relatable to or having any linkage with recommendation or decision of the appellant in his capacity as public servant,” the bench said, accepting the arguments of Rajasthan additional advocate general Sansriti Pathak. Writing the judgement, Justice Anjaria said, “In the facts and circumstances of the case, therefore, the act of the appellant does not fall within the protective umbrella of Section 17A of the Act. It is also known as Periya Kovil, RajaRajeswara Temple, and Rajarajesvaram.
It is one of the largest temples in India and is an example of Dravidian architecture during the Chola period. It was constructed under the patronage of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE. The entire temple structure is made out of granite.
The construction of the temple out of granite was done without mortar. The temple stands amidst fortified walls that were probably added in the 16th century. The central tower, or vimana, is 66 m high and is the tallest in the world.
It is also the most ornate and elaborate, with intricate carvings and paintings. The Kumbam (the apex or the bulbous structure on the top) at the top of vimana is carved out of a single rock and weighs around 80 tons. There is a big statue of Nandi (sacred bull), carved out of a single rock measuring about 4.9 m long and 4.0 m high at the entrance.
The temple complex is surrounded by two concentric rectangular enclosures (prakarams) with massive walls. These enclosures are entered through ornate gateways known as gopurams. India's services trade surplus, which plays a crucial role in offsetting the country's merchandise trade deficit, is showing signs of pressure as services imports grow faster than exports, according to an ICICI Bank research report.
The emerging concern is that faster growth in services imports could reduce the net foreign exchange earnings generated by India's services sector, weakening an important cushion against the country's large merchandise trade deficit.
According to the bank's research report, net services exports declined 10 per cent year-on-year to USD 16.9 billion in September 2026. The report stated that "net services exports saw a much sharper decline of 10% YoY to USD 16.9bn."
The contraction came as gross services exports fell 0.9 per cent year-on-year to around USD 36 billion, while services imports increased 8.9 per cent to approximately USD 19 billion.
This divergence indicates that India's spending on services purchased from overseas is growing faster than the earnings generated through services sold to foreign markets.
India's services exports, including information technology, financial, business and professional services, have traditionally helped compensate for the country's higher spending on imported goods. However, when services imports grow faster than exports, the resulting surplus narrows, reducing the amount available to offset the merchandise trade gap.
The trend assumes significance even as India's merchandise exports registered strong growth of 23 per cent year-on-year in September, highlighting differing trends in the country's goods and services trade performance.
However, the September decline does not yet suggest a sustained weakening of India's services trade position. According to ICICI Bank, cumulative net services exports increased 4 per cent year-on-year to USD 103 billion during April-September 2026, compared with an average monthly surplus of USD 17.1 billion in the first half of FY27 against USD 16.5 billion a year earlier.
The contrasting monthly and half-year trends indicate that while the services sector continues to provide substantial support to India's external trade position, sustaining that cushion will depend on export earnings keeping pace with the country's growing services import bill.
The September figures remain provisional, with subsequent data releases expected to provide greater clarity on whether the slowdown is temporary or reflects a broader moderation in services trade.

Chennai: Flaying Karnataka officials for wilful disobedience and non-compliance with its orders to prevent pollution of the Thenpennai River, the National Green Tribunal has sought individual explanations from authorities concerned. Exercising powers under the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal has ordered notices to the Karnataka chief secretary, the Bengaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB) chairperson, and the heads of the forest and municipal administration departments, directing them to explain the non-compliance before the next hearing on Nov 11. The Tribunal noted that several directions were passed in 2021 and 2022 to prevent pollution of water at Kelavarapalli dam, including holding periodic review meetings at least once in 2 months and setting up sewage treatment plants (STP), and the matter was taken up for review on several occasions. sum.text:
Eligible first-time employees joining the formal workforce can receive an incentive of up to ₹ 15,000 under the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY). The scheme, administered through the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), aims to encourage formal employment by rewarding eligible workers entering the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) system for the first time.
However, the benefit is subject to eligibility and service conditions. Employees cannot assume they will automatically receive ₹ 15,000 simply by joining a company. The incentive is linked to eligible EPF wages, continued employment and compliance with the scheme’s requirements.
The scheme covers eligible jobs created between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027. Employees earning monthly wages of up to ₹ 1 lakh may qualify, subject to the other conditions. The incentive is equivalent to one month’s eligible EPF wage, capped at ₹ 15,000.
To qualify under Part A of PM-VBRY, an employee must be joining the formal workforce as a first-time EPF member. The scheme covers eligible employees joining establishments between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027, provided they meet the prescribed membership, wage and employment conditions.
Employees should check their EPF membership history and ensure that their employer is depositing contributions and filing the required Electronic Challan-cum-Returns (ECRs). Meeting the salary limit alone does not guarantee eligibility.
The incentive is paid in two instalments, subject to the scheme's conditions. The first instalment is available after six months of continuous service, while the second is linked to completing 12 months of service and the prescribed financial literacy programme.
The amount is based on eligible wages, so not every employee will receive the maximum. Further, the second instalment is not necessarily paid as immediately withdrawable cash. Under the scheme guidelines, it is to be placed in an appropriate savings instrument or deposit account for a specified period.
Completing the prescribed financial literacy programme is a condition for receiving the second instalment. Employees who complete six months of service may qualify for the first payment, but they must also meet the 12-month service requirement and complete the programme to qualify for the second.
